summary: Defines how Trickle ICE, the incremental delivery of connection candidates, is used with the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP). Doing so lets SIP calls begin connectivity checks sooner and shortens session setup. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This document describes how a SIP call can pass the network address clues it needs in small batches, over SIP INFO requests, instead of waiting until every clue has been collected. Connectivity checks then run while the remaining clues are still arriving.

how does trickle ice work with sip

subtitle: How SIP phones can share network address clues in small batches, so calls start before every clue is in.

tldr.problem: With plain ICE, both sides of a SIP call gather every possible network address before the call can start, which makes the call wait for the slowest discovery.
tldr.mechanism: The two sides exchange address clues incrementally in SIP INFO requests, each carrying the candidates gathered so far, while the connectivity checks run alongside.
tldr.outcome: The call can start as soon as one usable pair of addresses is found. RFC 8840 is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 9725.

sections.title: Why Trickle ICE Needs SIP
sections.content:
The Interactive Connectivity Establishment protocol of RFC 8445 describes a mechanism for traversing Network Address Translators, made of three main phases. In the first phase an agent gathers a set of candidate transport addresses, meaning a source IP address, a port and a transport protocol. In the second phase these candidates are sent to a remote agent in the Session Description Protocol body of a SIP message, and the remote agent repeats the gathering procedure and sends its candidates back. In the third phase, which starts in parallel once the candidate information is available, connectivity between all the candidates in both sets is checked. Only once these phases have completed can both agents begin communication.

According to RFC 8445 those three phases happen consecutively and in a blocking way, which can introduce undesirable setup delay during session establishment. The Trickle ICE extension of RFC 8838 defines the generic semantics needed for these phases to happen in a parallel, non-blocking way, and so speeds up session establishment.

This specification defines a usage of Trickle ICE with the Session Initiation Protocol. It describes how ICE candidates are exchanged incrementally using SIP INFO requests of RFC 6086, and how the Half Trickle and Full Trickle modes of RFC 8838 are to be used by SIP user agents depending on their expectations for support of Trickle ICE by a remote agent. The document defines a new Info Package for use with Trickle ICE, together with the corresponding media type, SDP attribute and SIP option tag.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up a call through a router that rewrites addresses means finding one address pair that works from each side. Finding all of them first, then testing them, makes the caller wait. Trickle ICE finds them a few at a time and tests them as they arrive.

sections.title: How Candidates Are Trickled
sections.content:
When ICE is used for SIP according to RFC 8839, the candidates are exchanged solely through the SDP offer and answer procedure of RFC 3264. This specification defines an additional mechanism where candidates can be exchanged using SIP INFO messages and a newly defined Info Package. That also allows candidates to be sent in parallel to an ongoing offer and answer negotiation, or after it has finished.

Typically, where Trickle ICE is fully supported, the offerer sends an INVITE request containing a subset of candidates. Once an early dialog is established, the offerer can continue sending candidates in INFO requests within that dialog. An answerer can send ICE candidates in INFO requests within the dialog established by its provisional response.

To benefit from the full potential of Trickle ICE and reduce session establishment latency as far as possible, Trickle ICE agents need to generate SDP offers and answers that contain incomplete and potentially empty sets of candidates. Such offers and answers can only be handled meaningfully by agents that actually support incremental candidate provisioning, so support has to be confirmed before it is used.

Contrary to other protocols, where capability discovery in advance is widely implemented, the mechanisms that allow this for SIP, a combination of user agent capabilities of RFC 3840 and Globally Routable User Agent URIs of RFC 5627, have only seen low levels of adoption. SIP user agents therefore have no obvious means of verifying that their peer will support incremental candidate provisioning.

From the point of view of SIP middleboxes and proxies, the offer and answer exchange for Trickle ICE looks partly similar to the one for regular ICE, but the INFO messages have to be considered as well to have the full picture of the candidate exchange. From an architectural point of view, exchanging candidates through SIP INFO requests can be represented as signalling between the ICE modules rather than between the offer and answer modules of the user agents. The INFO requests do not affect the state of the offer and answer transaction other than by providing additional candidates, so they are not considered offers or answers. Nevertheless, candidates that have been exchanged in INFO requests SHALL be included in subsequent offers or answers, and the version number in the "o=" line of that subsequent offer must be incremented by one.
sections.plainLanguage: The candidates do not have to wait for the offer and answer to finish. They travel in separate messages that the offer and answer machinery treats as extra information, not as a new offer.

sections.title: The Offer, the Answer and the INFO Requests
sections.content:
Trickle ICE agents exchange ICE descriptions compliant with RFC 8838 through the offer and answer procedure and through INFO request bodies, which requires five SIP-specific extensions. Agents MUST indicate support for Trickle ICE by including the SIP option tag "trickle-ice" in a SIP Supported: header field in all SIP INVITE requests and responses, and by including the ice-option "trickle" in all SDP offers and answers. Agents MAY include any number of candidates, from zero to the complete set, in their initial offer or answer; when the complete set is already in the initial offer it is called Half Trickle. Agents MAY exchange additional candidates in INFO requests within an existing INVITE dialog usage, including an early dialog, and MUST be prepared to receive them there. And agents MAY exchange additional candidates before the answerer has sent the answer, provided that an invite dialog usage is established at both agents.

If an offerer wants to send its initial offer before knowing any candidate for one or more media descriptions, it MUST set the port to the default value 9 for those media descriptions. If it does not want to include the host IP address in the corresponding "c=" line, for example for privacy reasons, it SHOULD include a default address, the IPv4 address 0.0.0.0 or the IPv6 equivalent ::. It then obviously cannot know the RTCP transport address, so it MUST NOT include the "rtcp" attribute, which avoids a potential ICE mismatch for that address. It MUST include the "ice-options:trickle" attribute, and MUST include a "mid" attribute in each "m=" line, which identifies the line a candidate belongs to and helps when several media lines are present and gathering may happen in a different order from the lines. The same rules apply to the initial answer.

To start trickling, two conditions have to be satisfied: Trickle ICE support at the peer must be confirmed, and a dialog must have been created. For an agent that sent an offer in an INVITE and received the answer in a reliable provisional response, both are guaranteed once the reliable response is acknowledged, and the offerer and the answerer can then freely trickle within the newly established dialog.

The situation is more delicate for an answerer that sent its answer in an unreliable provisional response, because it does not know whether the response was received or whether the offerer's dialog has entered the early state. To clear the ambiguity, the answerer retransmits the provisional response with the exponential backoff timers of RFC 3262. Those retransmissions must cease on receipt of an INFO request carrying a "trickle-ice" Info Package body, on receipt of any other in-dialog request from the offerer, or on transmission of the answer in a 2xx response. The offerer cannot send in-dialog requests until it receives a response, so the arrival of such a request proves that the response arrived.

The offerer MUST send a Trickle ICE INFO request as soon as it receives an SDP answer in an unreliable provisional response. That request must repeat the candidates already provided in the offer, since the first could be a Half Trickle offer that already carries all the candidates, and the second could be a Full Trickle offerer that is still gathering. When Full Trickle is used and newly learned candidates are available, the offerer SHOULD also deliver them in that request, unless it wants to hold some back for later. It SHOULD include an "end-of-candidates" attribute if candidate discovery has ended in the meantime.

Because the ability to convey arbitrary candidates in INFO bodies allows agents to trickle without actually sending an answer, agents can respond to an INVITE with provisional responses that carry no SDP answer, which establishes an early dialog. When the answer is finally sent it must repeat all the currently known and used candidates and may include newly gathered ones, and if that answer was already sent in an unreliable provisional response it must be repeated exactly in the 200 OK response. In that case the offerer must be prepared for receiving fewer candidates in the repeated answer than were exchanged by trickling, and MUST ignore the candidate information in that 200 OK response.
sections.plainLanguage: The offer may carry no addresses at all, using a placeholder port instead. Once both sides know the other supports trickling and a dialog exists, each side sends its addresses in small batches. The first INFO request repeats what was already sent, so that a lost or reordered message can be spotted.

sections.title: Discovering That the Peer Supports Trickling
sections.content:
SIP user agents are required by RFC 8838 to indicate their support of and intent to use Trickle ICE in their offers and answers with the "ice-options:trickle" attribute, and they MUST include the SIP option tag "trickle-ice" in a SIP Supported: or Require: header field. That makes discovery fairly straightforward for answerers, and for cases where offers are generated within existing dialogs, such as UPDATE or re-INVITE requests, where earlier SDP bodies have already provided the necessary information.

That information is of course not available when a first offer is being constructed, so three ways of addressing the problem are suggested.

  • Provisioning. In some deployments it is possible to know in advance that some or all reachable endpoints support Trickle ICE, for example when Session Border Controllers that support this specification connect to user agents that do not. An offerer that assumes Trickle ICE support MUST include a SIP Require: trickle-ice header field, so that if the assumption is wrong the failure is easy to track down and recoverable by resending the request without that header field.
  • Discovery with GRUUs. RFC 3840 lets user agents query for support of specific capabilities using OPTIONS requests, and support for GRUU lets SIP requests be addressed to a specific user agent rather than an arbitrary instance of an address of record. Combining the two with the "trickle-ice" option tag lets an agent learn the capabilities of a specific instance and then address it directly with an INVITE that requires Trickle ICE. The instance identifier can be learned through presence and then queried with an OPTIONS request, or an OPTIONS request can be sent to the address of record and the response inspected for support of both GRUU and Trickle ICE. Using a GRUU means the request can only go to that one device, which prevents forking.
  • Fall back to Half Trickle. Where none of the other mechanisms is acceptable, agents use the Half Trickle mode of RFC 8838. They then start the session as they would with ICE for SIP in RFC 8839, gathering the candidates in a blocking way and sending them all in the offer. The blocking nature means some latency accumulates, and agents are advised to anticipate it where possible, for example when user actions indicate that a call is likely. Half Trickle results in offers compatible with both ICE for SIP endpoints and legacy endpoints.

Once a single offer or answer has been exchanged within a dialog, support for Trickle ICE will have been determined, so no further use of Half Trickle is needed in that dialog and all subsequent exchanges can use Full Trickle.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the first offer there is no way to know whether the other end understands trickling. The document gives three ways out: assume it does and insist on it, ask the other end directly using an OPTIONS request and a device-specific address, or fall back to gathering everything first.

sections.title: The INFO Request Body
sections.content:
Whenever new ICE candidates become available, agents encode them in "candidate" attributes as described in RFC 8839. The use of SIP INFO requests happens within the context of the Info Package, and the media type of the payload MUST be set to "application/trickle-ice-sdpfrag".

Neither the "candidate" nor the "end-of-candidates" attribute says which media line a candidate belongs to, so the body uses pseudo "m=" lines. These follow the SDP syntax for "m=" lines and are linked to the corresponding line in the offer or answer through the identification tag in a "mid" attribute. A pseudo "m=" line carries no other meaning, so the receiving agent MUST ignore any remaining content of it that this document does not define. That keeps these bodies from interfering with the offer and answer procedures.

When sending the INFO request the agent MAY include the same content in the pseudo "m=" line as in the corresponding offer or answer line, if it already knows it. Because Trickle ICE may be decoupled from the offer and answer negotiation, the content might be unknown, and in that case the agent MUST use these defaults: the media field is "audio", the port value is 9, the proto value is "RTP/AVP", and the fmt field appears only once and is set to 0. Agents MUST include a pseudo "m=" line and a "mid" attribute for every line whose candidate list they intend to update, and the "mid" attributes MUST immediately precede the list of candidates for that line. All "candidate" or "end-of-candidates" attributes following a "mid" attribute, up to but excluding the next pseudo "m=" line, belong to the line that the tag identifies.

An "end-of-candidates" attribute before the first pseudo "m=" line means that trickling has ended for the whole session, while a media-level one means it has ended for that line only.

All INFO requests MUST carry the "ice-pwd" and "ice-ufrag" attributes, which map them to a specific ICE generation, and an agent MUST discard any received INFO request whose attributes do not match the current ICE negotiation session. Those two attributes MUST appear at the same level as in the offer and answer exchange, so session-level ones come at the beginning of the payload and media-level ones follow the corresponding pseudo "m=" line.

Because an agent is not fully aware of the state of the ICE negotiation session at its peer, it MUST include all currently known and used local candidates in every INFO request, repeating in the same order the candidates previously sent under the same combination of "ice-pwd" and "ice-ufrag", with newly gathered candidates added at the end. Repeating them costs some overhead but makes loss and reordering detectable through the CSeq header field. On receipt, agents MUST first identify and discard the candidates already received in previous INFO requests or in the offer and answer exchange, treating two candidates as equal when their IP address, port, transport and component ID are the same, and then forward the new candidates to the ICE agents in the same order as they arrived.
sections.plainLanguage: The body of each INFO request is a small piece of the session description, holding the addresses for each media stream. Every request repeats the addresses already sent and adds any new ones, so a lost request can be recovered from the next one.

sections.title: The Info Package and the Option Tag
sections.content:
The choice of SIP INFO requests as the carrier is based primarily on their lightweight nature. Once a dialog has been established, INFO requests can be exchanged in both directions with no restrictions on timing or frequency and no risk of collision. A critical fact is that sending candidates in one direction is entirely uncoupled from sending them in the other, so each direction can use a stream of INFO requests that is not correlated with the other. Since each request cumulatively includes the contents of all previous ones in that direction, the ordering between requests need not be preserved.

UPDATE and the other offer and answer mechanisms, by contrast, assume that the messages in each direction are tightly coupled with the messages in the other. Offer and answer is defined as a strictly sequential mechanism, so there can be at most one active exchange at a time, and both sides cannot send offers simultaneously or generate several offers before receiving an answer. Using UPDATE for candidate transport would therefore mean keeping a candidate pool at every agent, with the complexity that brings. The sequential nature also makes glare impossible to prevent, and the procedure for handling it invalidates both offers and requires a retry after a backoff of between 0 and 4 seconds, which would make Trickle ICE slower rather than faster. INFO messages avoid all of that, and using in-dialog INFO messages also guarantees that candidates are delivered between the same entities that are initiating the session.

The Info Package token name is "trickle-ice", and the document defines no Info Package parameters and no usage restrictions. The option-tag construct of the SIP grammar is extended with the option tag "trickle-ice", and entities that support this specification MUST place it in a SIP Supported: or Require: header field in all SIP INVITE requests and responses, and also when responding to or generating a SIP OPTIONS request. Entities implementing the specification MUST include a payload of type "application/trickle-ice-sdpfrag" in SIP INFO requests, and the payload is used to convey the SDP-encoded ICE candidates.

Because IP addresses may be gathered rapidly, an agent with many network interfaces could create a high rate of INFO requests if every newly detected candidate were trickled individually. An implementation MUST aggregate ICE candidates when an unreliable transport such as UDP is used, and a Trickle ICE agent MUST NOT have more than one INFO request pending at a time. Over TCP that is no longer a problem for the network, but it can remain one for SIP proxies and other intermediaries forwarding the messages.
sections.plainLanguage: INFO requests were chosen because they are cheap and can go in both directions at once. Offer and answer cannot, because only one exchange can be open at a time. The document also limits how often the messages may be sent.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 6086, RFC 8838 and RFC 8839 apply. The document clarifies how those specifications are used together for trickling candidates and does not create additional security risks.

The new Info Package "trickle-ice" and the new media type "application/trickle-ice-sdpfrag" do not introduce additional security considerations when used in the context of Trickle ICE. Both are not intended to be used for other applications, so any security considerations for their use in other contexts is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no security rules of its own. The rules of the ICE and INFO specifications it builds on apply unchanged.

items.title: Provision it
items.text: The deployment knows the far end supports trickling. The offerer adds a Require: trickle-ice header field so a wrong assumption fails loudly.

items.title: Ask the far end
items.text: An OPTIONS request asks a device-specific address whether it supports the trickle-ice option tag, and the INVITE then goes to that device.

items.title: Fall back to Half Trickle
items.text: Gather everything first and send it in the offer. Works with any peer, but the caller waits for the gather to finish.

items.label: SIP Info Package
items.desc: The Info Package that carries the candidate bodies in INFO requests.

items.label: SIP option tag
items.desc: Put in a Supported: or Require: header field to say the user agent supports trickling.

items.label: Media type
items.desc: The media type of the INFO request body that holds the candidates.

items.label: SDP attribute
items.desc: A property attribute with no value, saying that no further candidates will be trickled.
